The minters mapping is checked in the mint function (YFII.mint(address,uint256)), allowing only addresses marked as minters to mint tokens.
Since the governance address can add or remove minters, it can effectively control who has the ability to mint tokens, leading to potential hidden minting capabilities.

This means that the governance address can grant minting privileges to any address, allowing for the creation of tokens without any checks on the total supply or balances, which fits the definition of MINT.
The function YFII.addMinter(address) allows the addition of new minters without any restrictions, as it is a public function with no modifiers.
Once a new minter is added, they can call the YFII.mint(address,uint256) function, which checks if the caller (msg.sender) is in the minters mapping.
If the caller is a minter, they can mint tokens to any address without any balance checks, effectively allowing them to increase the balance of any address they choose.
This behavior aligns with the definition of Hidden Mint, as it allows privileged users to create tokens out of thin air and assign them to arbitrary addresses.
The function YFII.removeMinter(address) allows a privileged user to remove an address from the minters list.
This directly affects the ability of the minters to call the YFII.mint(address,uint256) function, as the minting process requires the caller to be in the minters mapping.
If a minter is removed, they can no longer mint tokens, effectively limiting their ability to participate in the minting process.
This control over who can mint tokens creates a scenario where the privileged user can restrict or enable minting for others, thus classifying it as a LIMIT behavior.
